words.technical: The computed trend is only mildly positive because the horizons disagree: the one-month and one-year components point up while the half-year component points down, and the 21-day reading sits at about half a standard deviation above trend. After the week's near-3% fall the price is almost exactly mid-way through its one-year range, and daily volatility above 1.6% remains high for this metal. The stance is Flat, with the flip to Hold nearly 3% above the market — a level the week's rally attempt on Thursday did not come close to.
words.macro: Gold opened Friday at its highest of the week after a Fed governor said on Thursday he would support holding rates in September if the August inflation data keep improving, which pulled market odds of a hike from above 60% to roughly a coin flip. The August jobs report then landed at 162,000 against a consensus near 55,000 with unemployment steady at 4.1%, the two-year yield jumped to its highest since January 2025, hike odds climbed back above 50%, and spot gold gave up more than 2% to settle near $4,390. The metal is being squeezed by the same two forces all week — a stronger dollar and the prospect of tighter policy — and next Thursday's CPI is now the release that decides the September meeting.
words.long_term: The structural case — official-sector accumulation and deteriorating fiscal arithmetic in the large economies — is unchanged, and it is being tested this quarter by a central bank that may tighten rather than ease.

eoy_scenarios.central: August CPI is soft enough to keep the Fed on hold, real yields stop rising, and gold consolidates the summer's gains inside the central band without a new catalyst in either direction.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Fed holds and the debasement worry that drove the August rally returns as oil-fed inflation erodes real returns elsewhere, carrying gold through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hot CPI print delivers a September hike and the market begins pricing a cycle, real yields grind higher through the autumn and the leveraged length built in August unwinds through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: Silver's trend picture is weaker than the headline score suggests: the one-month and one-year components are positive but both the quarter and half-year components are negative, and the price now sits in the lower third of its one-year range after a near-6% weekly fall. Daily volatility near 2.8% is the highest of the metals and the main reason the computed stance stands aside at Flat, with the flip to Hold roughly 7% above the market.
words.macro: Silver started the week sliding as the weekend's US strikes on Iran pushed oil higher and made a September rate rise feel inevitable, with futures near $65.40 on Tuesday morning, then recovered with gold on Thursday's Fed-governor comments before easing again Friday to around $66.70. Despite a gain of more than 70% over twelve months the metal is now down about 6% year-to-date, a measure of how far the January peak above $110 has unwound, and the gold/silver ratio has drifted back toward 67. One commodity strategist summed up the week's cross-current: energy and industrial metals are benefiting from scarcity while gold and silver are temporarily paying the price for tighter monetary conditions and a stronger dollar.
words.long_term: The structural deficit story — electrification and AI-related industrial demand against constrained mine supply — is intact, but silver's higher beta means it takes the policy shocks harder than gold in both directions.

eoy_scenarios.central: Industrial demand holds a floor while the policy threat caps the speculative premium, and silver chops inside the central band with the ratio to gold broadly stable.
eoy_scenarios.upside: A Fed hold and a renewed debasement bid bring the leveraged buyers back and the metal outpaces gold on the way up, clearing the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A September hike and a firmer dollar keep draining the speculative length, and with the price already in the lower third of its range the unwind carries it through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: Crude carries the sharpest short-term momentum on the board after a 9%-plus week — the 21-day reading is above +1.7 standard deviations — while the quarter and half-year components are flat and the one-year component positive. The price sits in the upper part of its one-year range and daily volatility near 2.8% remains war-elevated. The stance is Hold, with the flip back to Flat about 3% below the market, so an ordinary give-back after a move this size would test it.
words.macro: WTI posted its steepest weekly gain since mid-July — Brent was up more than 7% and WTI more than 10% at one point on Friday before both eased into the close — after US strikes killed and wounded dozens in the fiercest US-Iran clashes since July, now in the war's seventh month, and Iran expanded its list of vessels it will fine or seize in the Strait of Hormuz. Only four commodity vessels transited the strait on Thursday against a ten-day average of about fifteen, US diesel averages hit record highs on top of Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and one bank lifted its short-term Brent forecast to $95 while another raised its third-quarter view to $86. Capping the move: Iraq lifted August exports to about 2.34 million barrels a day from 1.35 million in July, Saudi Arabia left its Asian crude price unchanged, and talk of a path to a Ukraine settlement weighed late in the week.
words.long_term: The market still carries a structural war-risk premium — Brent is up almost 60% this year and Gulf flows remain far below pre-war levels — so the long-term range stays wide and headline-driven in both directions, with inventory buffers now thinner than in the spring.

eoy_scenarios.central: Hormuz stays erratic but open, Iraqi and non-Gulf supply keeps growing into the gap, and crude drifts inside the central band with the war premium expressed mostly in diesel and product spreads.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The fighting reaches energy infrastructure or the strait closes to all but approved traffic, the supply-loss scenario the market discounted in August returns, and crude breaks above the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A ceasefire or shipping arrangement deflates the war premium while high prices and rising rates cut demand, and crude falls through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: Bitcoin keeps a strong computed trend with both the 21-day and quarter readings above +1.5 standard deviations, though the one-year component is slightly negative, and the price sits close to the middle of its one-year range. Daily volatility near 2.5% is ordinary for the asset. The stance stays Hold and the flip to Flat is nearly 6% below the market, room enough for a normal pullback.
words.macro: The coin rallied about 4% to above $80,000 and traded as high as $82,000, a four-month high, after a Fed governor said on Thursday he could back holding rates steady in September, taking the market-implied odds of a hike from above 63% earlier in the week to roughly even; US spot bitcoin funds took in about $730 million the same day. Friday's stronger-than-expected payrolls report pushed those odds back above 50% and the price back under $80,000, so the week finishes up about 2% with the rally faded rather than reversed. A September hold would add no liquidity, but it would lift the tightening risk that has capped rallies since the spring.
words.long_term: The structural picture is unchanged: institutional adoption and the debasement narrative support the asset across quarters, while its correlation with policy-sensitive risk assets keeps every Fed inflection a two-way event.

eoy_scenarios.central: The September meeting passes as a hold, the August high caps the market for a while, and bitcoin works sideways inside the central band with the trend intact.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Fed stands down and the debasement trade resumes, carrying the coin through its August high and above the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hike drains risk appetite, the mid-range support gives way, and the retreat extends through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: The index carries the strongest computed trend on the board, driven by the half-year and one-year components, while the 21-day reading is essentially flat after a week that went nowhere. The price sits in the top tenth of its one-year range and daily volatility near 0.7% is the lowest of the risk assets. The stance is Hold, but the flip level sits exactly at Friday's close, so any weekly close below this level would turn the stance to Sell — the thinnest margin on the board.
words.macro: The week was a round trip: the index rose more than 1% on Thursday to a record close as a Fed governor leaned toward a September hold and Treasury yields fell, then gave back most of it Friday, closing down 0.38% at 7,718.60 after August payrolls of 162,000 blew past estimates near 55,000 and the two-year yield hit its highest since January 2025. Futures traders now price a September hike at close to 58%, up from about 50% before the report, and one bank economist called the next decision finely balanced, with next week's CPI and PPI able to decide it. The S&P added about 0.1% on the week.
words.long_term: Earnings momentum and the AI investment cycle keep the long-term trend positive, but the index is priced for a policy path that does not include hikes, and the next two weeks decide whether that holds.

eoy_scenarios.central: Inflation data cooperate, the Fed holds, and the index grinds inside the central band on continued earnings growth with occasional rate scares.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The hike threat lifts entirely and growth stays solid, extending the record run through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A September hike compresses multiples at the top of the range and the retreat extends through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: The index sits in the upper part of its one-year range with every trend horizon positive, the longer ones strongly so, while the 21-day reading is close to flat. Daily volatility near 1.1% is well above the broad market's. As with the S&P, the stance is Hold with the flip level exactly at Friday's close, so a weekly close below this level would turn it to Sell.
words.macro: The week's tech story was a split verdict on AI chips: Broadcom reported revenue up 86% and AI chip sales up 221% year over year, yet the shares fell about 6% on Thursday because current-quarter revenue guidance of $34.8 billion came in just under consensus and gross margin is guided down to 73% from 78% a year earlier — a margin story, not a demand story, as Nvidia edged higher on the same report. The index still gained about 0.4% on the week after Thursday's 1.4% rally on the Fed-governor hold signal and Friday's give-back on the hot payrolls, with the two-year yield at its highest since early 2025.
words.long_term: The AI capital-spending cycle keeps earnings momentum in a handful of mega-caps; the index's long-term path is increasingly the path of that spending, and this week's Broadcom reaction shows the market has begun to price the cost of winning it, not just the revenue.

eoy_scenarios.central: AI earnings keep delivering while the Fed stays merely watchful, and the index grinds inside the central band on narrow leadership.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The spending cycle broadens beyond the mega-caps and policy stays benign, extending the rally through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hiking Fed compresses multiples exactly where the crowding is worst, and the narrow leadership that lifted the index takes it below the band on the way out.

week_summary: A week that swung on two Fed data points: a governor's Thursday speech leaning toward a September hold sent gold briefly back above $4,500 and bitcoin to a four-month high, then Friday's August payrolls — 162,000 against roughly 55,000 expected — put the hike back on the table, lifted the two-year yield to its highest since early 2025 and knocked gold and silver to weekly losses of about 3% and 6%. Oil was the outlier, up more than 9% on the week as US-Iran fighting resumed at its fiercest since July and Strait of Hormuz transits collapsed; the big US indices finished essentially flat, and the dollar index stands aside this week for next Thursday's ECB decision.
